az_linda_vista_wall.blurb: A compact wall on the Pusch Ridge side of the Santa Catalinas, reached from the northwest edge of Tucson. Six roped lines are bolted or protected by gear: four sport and two trad, running from an easy 5.7 through a couple of 5.9s to three at 5.10. The wall faces north and stays in shade for much of the day, and the slab carries patches of lichen. Expect a hike of around 20 minutes to a metal sign, then roughly another quarter hour up the Pusch Peak trail. A helmet is recommended. The wider Linda Vista zone holds a few days of moderate climbing and bouldering and feels more remote than its short approach suggests.

az_little_big_horn_wall.blurb: A small band of cliffs in Finger Rock Canyon, on the Santa Catalina Mountains above Tucson. It holds six single-pitch trad lines of about 100 feet, all graded 5.8 to 5.9+, and the anchors are easy to reach. The wall faces west. To get there, follow the Finger Rock Trail for about two miles, which takes around an hour, then walk five minutes off the trail to the base, which sits roughly 200 feet above a small overhang with a bench. Beyond the trailside bouldering, the canyon is treated as backcountry.

az_loose_goose.blurb: A small, rough crag in the Windy Ridge zone of the Catalina Highway on Mount Lemmon, just beyond Windy Point near mile marker 15.3. Six routes, mostly traditional with a couple of bolted ones, span 5.7 to 5.11, with the hardest being a bolted line. From the roadside pullout it is about a four-minute walk down a cairned climbers' trail to the outcrops. At this elevation summers run warm and winters cold, so spring and fall tend to suit the zone best.

az_matterhorn.blurb: A small, tidy miniature mountain at the top end of the Windy Ridge zone on the Catalina Highway, near mile marker 15.7. It has six routes, mostly trad with one bolted line. The grades range widely: a pair of 5.4s, then a 5.6, 5.7 and 5.8, topped by a single 5.11 sport route. The summit itself is an easy one. The approach is about five minutes by way of washes and slabs to the foot of the wall. The rock beneath the overhang is described as questionable. Good bouldering lies just to the south.

az_green_mt_buttresses_gmb.blurb: A pair of buttresses in the Mid-Mountain zone of Mount Lemmon, at roughly 7,200 feet in cool ponderosa forest. It has six routes: five trad and one sport, from 5.6 up to 5.10, some of them multi-pitch. The route to the base starts at San Pedro Vista, following the Green Mountain trail for about ten minutes before leaving it for a ledge system. It feels rugged for a spot so near the road, since an old fire, erosion and fallen timber complicate the travel. Established lines have cleaned up nicely, but off-line expect lichen and loose rock.

az_swerve_boulder.blurb: A single large boulder in the Linda Vista bouldering zone on Pusch Ridge, at the northwest edge of Tucson. It sits higher up the hill than the main sector: keep walking past the first blocks and the dihedral, then head straight uphill. Six problems cover a very wide spread, from V4 to V11, and include several classics. One side is tall and handsome, reaching about 35 feet, while the opposite face is unexciting. The harder lines lean on crimps and sustained power endurance, with long moves and few rests.

az_sietch_tabr.blurb: A crag of Sedona sandstone, one of the sub-areas within the Capitol Butte North Face zone near Coffeepot Rock. It stands out as a dense cluster of single-pitch cracks, a rarity in this part of Coconino County. Six trad routes run from 5.10 to 5.11, and the cracks are often wide and a little scruffy, so it suits experienced desert climbers. Follow the Capitalist Pillar approach, then continue a couple of hundred feet along the base of the wall to a fixed handline in a flared corner. Belays are on an exposed hanging terrace with a cliff directly below, so use the belay bolts carefully.
